content: The Belchertown State School for the Feeble-Minded was established in 1922 in Belchertown, Massachusetts. It was located at 30 State Street and spanned an 876-acre campus, which included ten major buildings designed in the Colonial Revival architectural style by Kendall, Taylor, and Co. Unlike state hospitals, which were intended for individuals with mental illnesses, state schools like Belchertown were institutions for those deemed mentally defective. However, the term school was misleading, as these facilities generally did not provide any form of education. For the first four decades of its operation, Belchertown State School functioned with little external oversight. However, it was later revealed that the residents, some of whom had spent their entire lives in the institution, were subjected to severe mistreatment and abuse by the staff. Author Benjamin Ricci described the conditions as horrific, medieval, and barbaric. Medical professionals at the school often disregarded the mental capacities of the residents. For example, one doctor evaluated a patient solely based on their inability to speak or respond, concluding that the individual was an imbecile without further assessment. The staff working in the wards were overburdened, with dozens of patients under their care, leading to appalling treatment of the residents. Due to time constraints, proper hygiene and toilet care were neglected, leaving residents half-naked, rolling in their own excrement. Severely physically disabled individuals were confined to their beds all day without any form of stimulation or entertainment. Patients who could not feed themselves were force-fed by attendants, often in a rough manner that caused injuries. When patients needed to be moved, they were handled with such force that it frequently resulted in harm. The neglect and abuse led to disturbing behaviors among the residents, such as moaning in the hallways, smearing feces, or repeatedly banging their heads against walls. The facility also suffered from infestations of vermin. The conditions at Belchertown were partly a reflection of societal attitudes toward individuals with disabilities during the early 20th century. At that time, many families cared for disabled individuals at home when possible. However, during the 1920s and 1930s, state governments began creating specialized divisions to manage these populations. In Massachusetts, this responsibility fell to the Department of Mental Retardation. The medical field also began to develop expertise in treating individuals with disabilities, which influenced social policies. Despite this, many parents felt they had no choice but to send their children to institutions like Belchertown, as there were few alternatives for those with severe disabilities. During the 1960s, societal awareness of the rights of disabled individuals began to grow, influenced in part by the civil rights movement. In 1966, Massachusetts passed the Mental Health and Retardation Services Act, which aimed to transition from large institutions to community-based care systems. The appalling conditions at Belchertown were brought to public attention in 1971 through a newspaper article titled The Tragedy of Belchertown. This led to a lawsuit filed by parents of the residents. When the state Attorney General visited the facility, he described it as a hell hole. This lawsuit was the first of its kind against a state school, and it set a precedent for similar legal actions in Massachusetts in the following years. In 1975, Belchertown faced another lawsuit for denying its residents the right to vote, marking one of the earliest disability-related voting rights cases in the United States. In 1977, a legal case was brought on behalf of a 67-year-old resident with severe intellectual disabilities and leukemia to determine whether he should receive chemotherapy. Despite these legal challenges, the institution continued to operate for several more years before finally closing in 1992. In 1994, the site was added to the National Register of Historic Places. In recent years, efforts have been made to repurpose and memorialize the site. Foley Field was transformed into a baseball diamond for the local Little League team, and the overgrown cemetery, where graves were previously marked only by numbers, was cleaned and restored to honor the deceased residents by name. In 2001, the town designated the school property as an Economic Opportunity Area for 20 years, offering tax incentives to businesses willing to establish themselves on the site. For those seeking more information about Belchertown, Benjamin Ricci's book Crimes Against Humanity: A Historical Perspective provides a detailed account. Ricci, who sent his six-year-old son Bobby to live at the school without knowing the conditions, was involved in the initial 1972 lawsuit. Another book, I Raise My Eyes to Say Yes by Ruth Sienkiewicz-Mercer, offers vivid descriptions of life at Belchertown. Sienkiewicz-Mercer was a resident of the school during the 1960s and 1970s. In her book, she mentions a young male nurse who worked at Belchertown during that time and later became a junior senator from Massachusetts—John Kerry.
